dok_rationale: Part (c) weighs population shape, independence, and sample size to judge two normality claims and distinguish a model for sample means from a model for individuals.
stem: Individual commute times in a very large city are strongly right-skewed, with population mean $\mu=25$ minutes and standard deviation $\sigma=15$ minutes. Consider independent random samples.\par\smallskip \textbf{Rae:} ``Any average is approximately normal, even for $n=4$.''\par \textbf{Sol:} ``With this long right tail, $n=4$ may be too small; $n=40$ is more defensible.''
first_take: Which would you expect to smooth out the long commute times more: averaging 4 people or 40? Give one reason.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the population shape and state the population mean and standard deviation with units.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: For $n=4$ and $n=40$, calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\bar{x}$.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: In 3--4 sentences, decide whose claim is better supported. Use the population shape, independence, and the two sample sizes. Explain which distribution the CLT describes and why using a normal curve for averages of 4 could be unreliable.

answers.a: The population distribution of individual commute times is strongly right-skewed. Its mean is $\mu=25$ minutes and its standard deviation is $\sigma=15$ minutes.
answers.b: For either sample size, $\mu_{\bar{x}}=\mu=25$ minutes. For $n=4$, $\sigma_{\bar{x}}=15/\sqrt{4}=7.5$ minutes. For $n=40$, $\sigma_{\bar{x}}=15/\sqrt{40}\approx2.3717$ minutes, or about $2.37$ minutes.
answers.c: Sol's claim is better supported: a long right tail can remain when only four commute times are averaged. Independent samples of 40 make an approximately normal distribution of sample means more defensible by the CLT. The CLT describes sample means, not individual commute times. Using a normal curve for averages of 4 could give unreliable tail probabilities.

expectedElements.description: Rejects automatic normality at n=4 using population right skew.
Supports n=40 as more defensible using independence and the CLT, without claiming a universal guarantee.
Distinguishes sample means from individual times and explains why a small-sample normal tail can be unreliable.

scoringGuide.E: Meets all three checks with correct contextual reasoning; equivalent wording is acceptable.
scoringGuide.P: Shows at least one substantive correct check, but has an omission or error that prevents E.
scoringGuide.I: Shows none of the three checks with substantive correct reasoning; a choice alone is insufficient.

commonMistakes: Treating the central limit theorem as applying at every sample size
Saying the individual commute-time population becomes normal when n increases
Dividing the mean, rather than the standard deviation, by $\sqrt{n}$
Using the number of repeated samples instead of the observations per sample as $n$
